He was born in the Dragon Palace as a prince;
his parents, out of deep affection and esteem, offered their own bodies to feed the garuḍa.
He was then born in Jambudvīpa as the crown prince of a king.
He was named Nengshi (Capable of Giving).
As soon as he was born, he was able to seek out objects to give in charity until his storehouse became empty and insufficient.
Upon hearing it said that dragon pearls existed, he desired to enter the sea to seek them.
The parents said, "You are our only son;
you may freely bestow these stored goods as you wish," and so forth.
They set a date and traveled by sea with five hundred merchants.

Regarding the phrase "vying for attachment," etc., it is raised again as a further illustration.
In the second fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, within the critique of the three types of cultivation, it says:
"You should know this:
that which you previously practiced—the contemplations on impermanence, suffering, and so forth—is not the ultimate reality.
It is, for example, like a group of people bathing in a large pond during the springtime."
While playing on a boat, they lost a lapis lazuli gem in deep water.
At that time, all the people entered the water together,
vying with one another to seize tiles, gravel, grass, and wood.
Each person thought they had obtained a lapis lazuli bead, and having joyfully taken it out, they realized it was not the real one.
At that time, the precious gem was still within the water;
by the power of the gem, the water became completely clear and transparent.
Then the great assembly saw that the precious gem was indeed within the water,
like looking up at the form of the moon in the sky.
At that time, the people, by means of skillful power, entered the water slowly and calmly.
Even if one were to obtain the jewel,
one should nevertheless not cultivate [notions of] impermanence, suffering, and so forth as being ultimate reality.
Zhan’an said:
The spring season, characterized by its pleasantness, is used as a metaphor for the realm of desire;
"all people" refers to those who are heedless;
and the "great pond" is a metaphor for birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Bathing is like anger and pride;
riding in a boat is like various karmas;
and sporting about is like the fruits of craving.
The loss of the treasure is a metaphor for lack of understanding;
entering the water is a metaphor for the initial teaching;
and searching for it is a metaphor for the three inferior practices.
The metaphors of tiles and stones illustrate the inferior threefold cultivation;
each gives rise to the notion of attaining nirvāṇa,
and because they harbor this internally, it is called "joy."
Because he praised the Buddha, it is said that he "carried [the teaching] out.
Thus we know that this was not a literal departure; rather, it serves as a metaphor for constant understanding.
